Title: Git Commands You'll Use Daily, Explained Simply
Desc: Learn the most useful Git commands that developers use every day. Understand what each command does, when to use it, and how it fits into a modern development workflow.
Author: Core Lord
Data:
## Git is one of the most important tools in modern software development. Whether you're building websites, mobile apps, APIs, or open-source projects, Git helps you track changes, collaborate with others, and safely manage your code.

The good news is that most developers use a relatively small set of Git commands every day.

In this guide, you'll learn the essential Git commands, what they do, and when to use them.

---

## Why Git Matters

Before Git, developers often copied folders like:

```text
project-final
project-final-v2
project-final-v3-real-final
```

Git solves this problem by providing:

* Version history
* Collaboration tools
* Safe experimentation
* Change tracking
* Easy rollbacks

It has become the industry standard for version control.

---

## Check Your Repository Status

One of the most frequently used commands is:

```bash
git status
```

This shows:

* Modified files
* New files
* Deleted files
* Staged changes
* Current branch

Example output:

```text
modified: index.html
modified: style.css
```

Many developers run `git status` dozens of times per day.

---

## View Commit History

To see previous commits:

```bash
git log
```

A cleaner version:

```bash
git log --oneline
```

Example:

```text
a4d7f8c Fix navbar alignment
c9f1e2a Add dark mode toggle
f2b8d11 Initial project setup
```

This makes history easier to read.

---

## Stage Files for Commit

Git uses a staging area.

To stage a file:

```bash
git add index.html
```

To stage all changes:

```bash
git add .
```

Think of staging as selecting which changes should be included in your next commit.

---

## Save Changes With a Commit

Once files are staged:

```bash
git commit -m "Add responsive navigation menu"
```

A commit acts like a snapshot of your project.

Good commits:

* Describe what changed
* Are short and clear
* Focus on one logical change

Avoid:

```bash
git commit -m "stuff"
```

Better:

```bash
git commit -m "Fix mobile navigation overflow issue"
```

---

## Create a New Branch

Branches allow you to work on features without affecting the main codebase.

Create a branch:

```bash
git branch feature-login
```

Switch to it:

```bash
git checkout feature-login
```

Modern Git combines both actions:

```bash
git checkout -b feature-login
```

Or:

```bash
git switch -c feature-login
```

This is commonly used when starting a new feature.

---

## Switch Between Branches

Move to another branch:

```bash
git switch main
```

Or:

```bash
git checkout main
```

This lets you move between different lines of development.

---

## Merge a Branch

After completing a feature:

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature-login
```

Git combines the changes from the feature branch into the main branch.

This is one of the most common collaboration workflows.

---

![Git branching and merging workflow diagram](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1516321318423-f06f85e504b3)

## Download Remote Changes

Fetch updates from the remote repository:

```bash
git fetch
```

This downloads information without changing your local files.

Useful when you want to inspect updates before applying them.

---

## Pull Latest Changes

Most developers use:

```bash
git pull
```

This command:

1. Downloads changes
2. Merges them into your branch

Always pull before starting work on a shared project.

---

## Upload Changes

Push commits to a remote repository:

```bash
git push
```

First push of a new branch:

```bash
git push -u origin feature-login
```

After that:

```bash
git push
```

This uploads your commits to platforms like GitHub.

---

## See File Differences

View changes before committing:

```bash
git diff
```

This helps verify modifications.

Example output:

```diff
- color: blue;
+ color: green;
```

Useful for catching mistakes before commits.

---

## Restore Changes

Discard local modifications:

```bash
git restore index.html
```

Restore everything:

```bash
git restore .
```

Be careful.

Restored changes cannot easily be recovered if they were never committed.

---

## Remove a File

Delete a tracked file:

```bash
git rm old-file.js
```

Then commit the removal:

```bash
git commit -m "Remove unused legacy file"
```

---

## Rename a File

Rename a file while preserving history:

```bash
git mv old-name.js new-name.js
```

Git tracks the rename operation.

---

![Software developer working with Git and GitHub](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1498050108023-c5249f4df085)

## Undo the Last Commit

Keep changes but remove the commit:

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

Completely remove commit and changes:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

Use the hard reset carefully because it can permanently remove work.

---

## Clone an Existing Repository

Download a project:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/user/project.git
```

Git creates a local copy of the repository.

This is often the first command used when joining a project.

---

## Check Current Branch

Display your current branch:

```bash
git branch
```

The active branch appears with:

```text
* main
```

Helpful when working with multiple branches.

---

## Daily Git Workflow Example

A typical day might look like:

```bash
git pull

git switch -c feature-search

git add .

git commit -m "Add search functionality"

git push -u origin feature-search
```

This workflow covers the majority of development tasks.

---

## Common Mistakes

### Committing Everything

Avoid:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Update"
```

Review changes first.

Use:

```bash
git status
git diff
```

---

### Working Directly on Main

Feature branches reduce risk.

Instead of:

```text
main
```

Use:

```text
feature-navbar
feature-auth
feature-search
```

---

### Ignoring Commit Messages

Poor commit messages make history difficult to understand.

Always describe the change clearly.

---

## Git Command Cheat Sheet

| Task             | Command                     |
| ---------------- | --------------------------- |
| Check status     | `git status`                |
| Stage files      | `git add .`                 |
| Commit changes   | `git commit -m "message"`   |
| View history     | `git log --oneline`         |
| Create branch    | `git switch -c branch-name` |
| Switch branch    | `git switch main`           |
| Merge branch     | `git merge branch-name`     |
| Pull updates     | `git pull`                  |
| Push commits     | `git push`                  |
| View changes     | `git diff`                  |
| Restore file     | `git restore file`          |
| Clone repository | `git clone URL`             |

---

## FAQ

### Do I need to learn every Git command?

No. Most developers use fewer than twenty commands regularly.

### Is Git the same as GitHub?

No.

Git is the version control system.

GitHub is a platform that hosts Git repositories.

### How often should I commit?

Commit whenever you complete a meaningful change.

Small, focused commits are easier to manage.

### Should beginners use branches?

Yes. Learning branches early helps build good habits.

### What command do developers use most?

Usually:

```bash
git status
```

because it quickly shows the current repository state.

---

## Final Thoughts

Git may seem intimidating at first, but daily development usually revolves around a small set of commands. Once you become comfortable with checking status, staging files, committing changes, creating branches, and syncing with remote repositories, you'll be able to handle most development workflows confidently.

Master these commands first, and you'll build a strong foundation for working with Git, GitHub, and collaborative software projects.
